chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Magic Mead
chapters.artPrompt: inside a crystal cave within a mountain, a tall wanderer in a dark blue cloak receiving three jars of golden mead from a fair maiden, warm glowing light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: There was a drink called the Magic Mead. Whoever tasted it grew wise, and could put wisdom into beautiful words that all would remember. The Dwarfs had brewed it out of the blood of Kvasir the Poet, whom they had killed in their caves. Through cruelty the Dwarfs gained it, and the Giants took it from them in turn. A Giant named Suttung hid the three jars of mead deep inside a mountain. He set his daughter to guard them, under a spell that gave her a horrible shape. And Odin the All-Father resolved to win the mead and give it to the sons of men.

New word: mead — a drink made from honey, golden and sweet. The Magic Mead of this story gives wisdom and the power of poetry. Whoever tastes it can put beautiful words to beautiful thoughts, and in the old North poets were loved almost as much as warriors.

So Odin traveled again as Vegtam the Wanderer, in his cloak of dark blue. He came to a field where nine thralls were mowing, and gave them a fine whetstone. They quarreled fiercely over it, and with their sharp scythes none was left to mow. Then the Wanderer went to the house of Baugi, the brother of Suttung. "Nine men's work will I do for you," he said, "if my fee is one draught of the Magic Mead." He did the work of nine men all the season. But when Baugi asked his brother for the fee, Suttung raged and would give none.

"You hold me to my bargain," said the Wanderer. So Baugi brought him to the mountain and bored a hole through the rock with a great drill. The Wanderer blew into the hole, and the dust flew back. "Not half way through yet, Giant," he said, and Baugi bored again. This time his breath went through. While Baugi looked up, Odin changed himself into a snake and slid into the hole. Behind the rock lay a hollow hall, lit by shining crystals. There sat a sad witch with long teeth, weeping for her lost youth and beauty.
In the crystal hall inside the mountain, fair Gunnloed gives Odin the three jars of the Magic Mead.

"Gunnloed," said Odin softly, for that was her name. He took her hands, and the red blood of youth came back into her cheeks. One kiss broke the spell, and she stood tall and fair as a Giant maiden should be. Then she gave him the three jars of the Magic Mead. For three days they talked together, and then Odin found hidden paths out of the mountain. He brought the jars into the world of men, and Gunnloed followed, singing of his might and beauty. And from that mead, they say, comes the gift of poetry among men.

Odin often travels the world in disguise under the name Vegtam the Wanderer. He wears a dark blue cloak and carries a staff, and Giants and men seldom guess who the quiet stranger is. He gave up his eye for wisdom, and he never stops seeking.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · Thor in the Giants' City
chapters.artPrompt: a red-bearded strong god gripping a hammer beside a huge drinking horn in a vast rough hall of stone, towering laughing giants all around, torchlight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Thor wished to try his strength against the Giants in their own City of Utgard, and Loki went with him. One night they stopped at a poor hut, for there was no food within. Thor killed his two goats for a meal, and told the family to lay the bones carefully on the skins. But the boy Thialfi broke one bone to gnaw the marrow. In the morning the goats stood alive again, and one limped badly. The boy wept and confessed. "Then you must serve me," said Thor, and Thialfi went with them.

New word: Utgard — the Giants' own city, deep in their cold country. Its buildings are huge and shapeless, like mountains and icebergs. Its name means the world outside, and its King is a master of magic.

On the moor they met a huge Giant named Skyrmir, who slept at noon with snores like falling cataracts. He gave them his wallet to open, but no one could untie the knots. Then Thor threw his hammer at the sleeping head three times. Each time the Giant only muttered that a leaf or an acorn had fallen. At parting, Skyrmir warned them that the folk of Utgard were far bigger and stronger than he. Thor marched into the Giants' City with his hammer in his hand.

In Utgard the Giant King set contests before his guests. First the boy Thialfi raced against a Giant youth named Hugi, and though Thialfi ran his swiftest, Hugi won easily. Then Loki took up an eating match against a huge eater called Logi. Plate after plate was emptied, but Logi had eaten the meat and the bones and the dishes too. Next Thor took the drinking horn and drank with all his might, yet it still seemed full.
Thor grips his hammer as the Giants laugh around the great drinking horn in the hall of Utgard.

"Then lift my cat from the ground," said the King. Thor heaved with all his strength, but only one paw of the great gray cat left the floor. Last of all, an old old woman came hobbling to wrestle with him. Her grip was like bands of iron, and Thor could only keep himself from falling on one knee. Angry and ashamed, Thor left the hall without a word and would not speak all the way home.

A trick of the eyes is called an illusion. Things look one way, but the truth is quite another. The wise King of Utgard was a master of such magic, and even Thor could not see through it while the games went on.

Long after, at a feast, a silent stranger rose, and all saw that he was the King of Utgard. "O Thor and O Loki," he said, "I will tell you the truth of those contests. I myself was Skyrmir on the moor, and your hammer blows struck a mountain, not me. Hugi was Thought itself, and no runner can beat Thought. Logi was Fire, which burns meat and bones and dishes together. The end of your horn lay in the sea, and the sea sank low when you drank. The cat was the great serpent that rings the world. The old woman was Old Age herself, and no one throws her." Then he cried that Thor was the mightiest of all beings, and the Gods rose up and cheered.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Thor and Thrym
chapters.artPrompt: a veiled bride far too tall and broad sitting at a wedding feast in a giant hall, a sly veiled bridesmaid whispering beside her, giants feasting at long tables, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One morning Thor reached for his hammer, and it was gone. Mjollnir was the defence of Asgard, and no one could tell where it was lost. Loki borrowed a dress of falcon feathers and flew at once to the land of the Giants. On a hillside he found Thrym, a stupid Giant with cunning streaks in him. "I have buried your hammer eight miles deep in the earth," Thrym said. "You shall never have it back, unless the Gods give me Freya for my wife."

New word: Mjollnir — Thor's great hammer, the strongest weapon the Gods own. It never misses its mark, and it always flies back to Thor's hand. That is why all Asgard was in danger while the hammer was lost.

The Gods sat in Council with bent heads when Loki came home. Give up Freya, whom the Giants had long sought in vain, or lose the hammer that guarded them all. Then Loki stood up with a smile. "Let us pretend to send Freya as a bride," he said. "Let one of the Gods go in her veil and dress." "Which of the Gods would do so shameful a thing?" they cried. "He who lost the hammer," said Loki, and all eyes turned to Thor.

Thor roared at first, but there was no other way. So the strongest of the Gods was dressed as a bride. A veil hid his beard, a garland crowned him, and a bunch of housekeeper's keys hung at his girdle. Loki, veiled as the bridesmaid, went beside him. Thrym welcomed them to his feast and would have lifted the veil. Loki whispered that a bride of Asgard must not be kissed before the company. Then the feast began. The bride ate a whole ox and eight salmon, and drank three barrels of mead. "What a lusty appetite our refined bride has," the Giants said.
Thor sits veiled as a bride beside Thrym while Loki nudges him and the wedding feast goes on.

Frigga, the wife of Odin, owns a dress of falcon feathers. Whoever wears it can fly through the sky like a great falcon. Loki has borrowed it more than once on his secret journeys, and it was Frigga herself who lent it this time.

A piece of the veil slipped, and Thrym saw glaring eyes. "Poor thing, she has not slept for eight nights for love of you," said quick Loki. "Now join hands with your bride, but first lay the hammer in her lap, as you promised." So Thrym, the stupidest of the Giants, brought Mjollnir into the hall and laid it in the bride's hands. The veil fell. Thor's blazing eyes flashed over the feast, and his fingers closed on the hammer. One blow brought the roof of the house down upon the Giants. And so the hammer was won back, and the wedding guests were buried in the ruin.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Children of Loki
chapters.artPrompt: a monstrous gray wolf straining against a thin silken cord on a rocky island, wary gods watching at a distance, stormy sea and dark sky, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Loki had a wife in the Giants' land, the witch Angerboda. Their children were not like the children of men. The Gods bade Loki bring them to Asgard, to see what forms they would take. The first showed himself as a fearful Wolf, and his name was Fenrir. The second showed itself as a Serpent, called Joermungand. The third took the form of a woman, and fear ran through Asgard at the sight of her. For one side of her was that of a living woman, and the other side was that of a corpse. Her name was Hela.

New word: Hela — the daughter of Loki who rules the realm of the dead, deep below the world. One side of her is a living woman, and one side is a corpse. Her dark hall lies in a land of mist and cold.

Odin took Hela and hurled her down below the world, to the dark land of the dead. There she reigned in a hall whose threshold was Precipice, whose table was Hunger, and whose bed was Care. Thor laid hold of the Serpent and flung it into the ocean that rings the world. But deep in the sea the Serpent grew and grew, until it lay all round the world of men. Men called it the Midgard Serpent, and they learned to dread it.

Fenrir the Wolf grew monstrous in Asgard, and only Tyr, the brave swordsman, dared to feed him. At last the Gods made a heavy iron chain and coaxed the Wolf to try his strength against it. Fenrir stretched himself a little, and the chain broke in two. A stronger chain fared no better. Then the Dwarfs were asked to forge a fetter no strength could break. Out of six strange things they made it. The roots of stones went into it, and the breath of a fish. The beards of women went in, and the noise of a cat's footfall. Last came the sinews of bears and the spittle of a bird. Gleipnir was its name, and it was soft as a silken ribbon.
The monstrous Wolf Fenrir strains against the silken cord Gleipnir while the Gods watch on the island.

Gleipnir is the magic fetter that binds the great Wolf. Though it is soft and thin as a silk ribbon, no strength in the world can break it. It was made by the Dwarfs out of six things that do not exist.

The Gods invited Fenrir to an island to make sport, and there they showed him the silken cord. "Such a slender thing," scoffed the Wolf. "There may be an enchantment in it," he growled. "I will let it go on me if one of you puts his hand in my mouth as a pledge." One by one the Gods stepped backward. Only Tyr came forward, and he put in his swordhand. Then the cord was bound fast, and no strength of the Wolf could break it. His jaws snapped shut, and Tyr's hand was gone. So Fenrir was chained to a rock far from Asgard, and he howls there still.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Baldur's Doom
chapters.artPrompt: a joyful crowd of gods hurling weapons at a radiant smiling god who stands unharmed in a bright meadow, a shadowy figure slipping away at the edge of the crowd, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Baldur the Well-Beloved was the fairest and kindest of all the Gods. White flowers on the earth were called by his name, and the birds sang it. He lived in a palace of peace where no crime had ever come. But sad dreams began to trouble his sleep, and little Hnossa dreamed a terrible dream too. She saw Hela, the Queen of the dead, saying that a lord of the Gods must come down to her. Odin's heart grew heavy. He rode down the dark roads to the land of the dead and called up a dead prophetess. "For Baldur, Odin's son, the bed is prepared and the seat is left empty," she said.

New word: Baldur — the best loved of all the Gods, the God of light and peace. No crime was ever told in his palace, and all white flowers bear his name. His mother Frigga loves him more than anything.

Frigga, the mother of Baldur, went through the world herself. She took an oath from fire and from water, from iron and all metals. Stones and great trees swore, and so did birds, beasts, and creeping things. Even poisons and diseases gave her their oath. All things swore to hurt Baldur never. Then gloom lifted from Asgard, and the Gods made a game of it. They flung battle-axes and stones and burning brands at Baldur, and everything fell harmlessly from him. Loud laughed the Dwarfs and the friendly Giants at the sport.

But Loki the Hater came among the crowd in the shape of an old woman. He went to Frigga's palace and asked, with kind words, what the game might mean. "All things have sworn to leave Baldur hurtless," said happy Frigga. "Only the little mistletoe passed me by, it was so small and weak." Loki hurried to the east side of Valhalla, where a young mistletoe bush grew on an oak. He broke off a spray and went back to the games. There stood Hoedur, Baldur's blind brother, alone and joyless, with nothing to throw.
Loki guides the blind God Hoedur's hand as he throws the small mistletoe twig toward bright Baldur.

"Take this twig and throw it," said Loki. "I will guide your hand." He put the mistletoe in the blind God's fingers and aimed the throw for him. The twig flew and struck Baldur on the breast, and Baldur fell down dead. A wailing rose around the Peace Stead, and Loki slipped away. Frigga asked who would ride down to Hela and ask a ransom for Baldur. Hermod the Nimble, brother of Baldur, mounted Odin's steed and rode the dark road for nine days and nights. Hela said that Baldur might come home if all things in the world wept for him.

Mistletoe is a small plant that grows high on the branches of trees. It has no root in the ground, so it seemed too weak to matter. That is why Frigga forgot to ask it for an oath, and in this story even the weakest thing matters.

Hermod found everything weeping, from the trees to the stones. But in a cave sat an old hag with blackened teeth, and she would not weep one tear. "Let Hela keep what she holds," she croaked, and she flew off as a crow. So the ransom failed, for that hag was Loki in another shape. Then the Gods made ready a funeral for their beloved. They laid Baldur on his great ship, and his gentle wife Nanna died of grief beside him. A Giantess gave one push and sent the burning ship into the sea. And in the flames men saw Odin bend and whisper into his son's ear. He spoke of a heaven above Asgard that no fire can reach.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · Loki's Punishment
chapters.artPrompt: a chained trickster bound to sharp rocks in a dark cavern, a faithful woman holding a cup above him beneath a hanging serpent, drops of venom glinting, storybook illustration

blocks.text: After Baldur's death, Loki hid from the wrath of the Gods. The crow that would not weep had been Loki in that shape too. He flew to the Giants and told them to build their great ship Naglfar. That ship was made of the nails of dead men. He crept as a lizard among the rocks of the fire land and made the Fire Giants glad. At last he built himself a house in the world of men. It had four doors, so that he could see danger coming from every side. Yet even Loki feared one thing, and he always kept ready his power to become a salmon.

New word: Naglfar — a ship the Giants are building out of the nails of dead men. It waits for the day of the last battle, when it will sail against the Gods. That is why men cut the nails of the dead.

The Gods searched the world over and found his house at last. Loki was weaving a net to catch fish, the first net that ever was. When he saw his enemies coming from four directions, he threw the net into the fire. Then he leapt into the river as a salmon. But one of the Gods studied the ashes and traced out the marks of the burnt net. From them he wove a net just like it. Down the river the Gods dragged their net, and Thor waded behind it. Loki leapt high over the net, and Thor caught him by the tail in both hands.

No fish had ever struggled so hard, but Thor held fast and dragged the salmon ashore. There Loki had to take his own form again. In a cavern the Gods bound him to three sharp-pointed rocks with cords of iron. Then Skadi, the Giant maid whose father had fallen from Asgard's wall, hung a venomous serpent above his head. Drop by drop the poison fell on his face, and minute by minute his anguish went on.
In the dark cavern, Siguna holds her cup above bound Loki while drops of venom fall from the serpent.

Then Siguna, the wife of Loki, came to stand beside him forever. She holds a cup above his face, and into the cup fall the serpent's drops of venom. Only when the cup is full must she turn aside to empty it. Then a drop falls on Loki, and he twists in his bonds and screams in agony. When he screams, men feel the earth quake and shudder. There Loki lies bound until the day of Ragnaroek, the Twilight of the Gods.

Siguna is the wife of Loki. Though her husband did great evil, she cannot leave him. In the cold cavern she holds the cup that saves him from the poison, drop by drop. Her pity is one of the saddest things in the old stories.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · The Twilight of the Gods
chapters.artPrompt: a green new world after a great battle, the World Tree sprouting fresh leaves, young gods and two awakened people gathering on a sunny plain, hopeful golden light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last the foretold time came. First there fell three winters with no spring between them, and brothers fought brothers for food. In the Iron Wood a witch fed a mighty Wolf on the bodies of the fallen. That Wolf grew big enough to swallow the Moon. Then a cock crew in each of three worlds. The rusty-red cock roused the dead, the crimson cock roused the Giants, and the golden cock roused Asgard. The earth shook, and the rock over Fenrir burst apart. Heimdall stood up and blew the Gialarhorn, and its sound rang through all the worlds. The doors of Valhalla swung open, and the Champions armed for the last battle.

New word: Ragnaroek — the Twilight of the Gods, the great last battle of the old stories. The evil powers and the hosts of Asgard meet on a wide plain. The old world ends there, but the story does not stop there.

Odin took counsel with the head of Mimir, which he drew from the Well of Wisdom. The head told him to meet the hosts of evil on Vigard Plain. Strike so hard, it said, that evil would never rise again. The riders of fire broke the Rainbow Bridge as they came. The Midgard Serpent reared out of the sea, and its flood swept the land. On the flood sailed the ship of the Giants, and the ship of the dead steered by Loki. "We will give our lives and let our world be destroyed," said Odin. "But we will battle so that these evil powers will not live after us."

Out of the ship of the dead sprang Fenrir the Wolf, his jaws stretching from earth to sky. Odin fought him and fell. Then Vidar the Silent set his foot on the Wolf's lower jaw and tore the jaws apart, and Fenrir died. Thor crushed the Midgard Serpent with one blow of Mjollnir. Then he staggered nine paces back, blinded by the serpent's venom, and there he fell. Loki and Heimdall fought each other, and each slew the other. Tyr fell before the hound Garm. Frey fought Surtur of the flaming sword, and with no sword in his hand, Frey fell. Then Surtur flung fire over all the earth, and the World Tree itself burned.
On the green new earth the young Gods gather while two people wake beneath the young World Tree.

Wolves caught the Sun and the Moon, and darkness came down on the world. Fire and flood swept over the burnt earth, and it seemed that everything had perished. But at last the seas drew back, and the earth rose green and beautiful again. A new Sun and a new Moon came, and no wolves chased them. Four young Gods stood on the highest peak, and Modi and Magni found Mjollnir the hammer again. Baldur came back from the land of the dead, gentle as before. In a deep wood two people had slept through the fire, and they woke to feed on the morning dew. From those two, Lif and Lifthrasir, men and women came again to spread over the green earth.

Lif and Lifthrasir are the two people who hide in the wood at the end of the old world. They sleep through the fire and wake to a green world. From them a new race of men and women grows, and their names mean Life and Striving after Life.
